title: Fear of death
hookLine: meeting fear of death with breath and kindness
tomorrow: if life is this short, what's the first thing to do with it?

lines: IS IT NORMAL TO BE SCARED OF DYING?
cards: Search bars hear what people won't say out loud. Late at night someone types: is it normal to be scared of dying? Long before search bars, a brahmin named Janussoni walked up to the Buddha with his answer already settled.
Everyone who has to die, he said, is afraid of death, terrified of it. No exceptions. It isn't a cruel claim.
It sounds like plain honesty. And the Buddha doesn't nod along.

teach.b: The story is in the Anguttara Nikaya, and the Buddha's answer is a sorting, not a scolding. Some people fear death and some don't, he says. Here is who fears.
One is still hungry for sense pleasures; when a serious illness comes, the thought arrives: the pleasures I love will be taken from me. He grieves and weeps and beats his breast.

teach.h: FOUR ROOTS: WANTING, BODY, REGRET, DOUBT.
teach.b: Another clings to the body itself: this body I love will be taken. A third has done harm and left good undone, and dreads where that leads. A fourth is in doubt about the teaching, with nothing firm to stand on.
Then the Buddha turns each one over.

The one who has let go of craving, who isn't clinging to the body, who has done good and harmed no one, who has no doubt about the teaching: when illness comes, that person isn't terrified. Notice what he doesn't say.
He doesn't call fear a failure, or say a good follower feels none.
He treats fear of death the way a doctor treats a fever: something with causes you can find. That's the part worth telling a friend tonight. The old answer here isn't be braver.
A root you can name is a root you can work with, slowly, across a life. Janussoni hears it and asks to be counted among the Buddha's followers.

how: Buddhist teachers who lead reflection on death sometimes pair it with recalling one's own good deeds and trust in the teaching, the same roots this sutta names; some temples offer this in classes on death and dying.

o: the dread of dying, with roots that can be named
a rare worry that only very old people have
a feeling that proves your practice has failed

games.q: who fears, and why — tap the pairs.
p: says everyone who must die fears death

s: a good Buddhist is supposed to feel no fear of death
the Buddha never calls fear a failure here. he names its roots so they can be worked with.
in the sutta, regret over harm done is one root of the fear
the one who has done harm and left good undone dreads where that leads.
the Buddha agrees with Janussoni that everyone fears death
he says some fear it and some don't, and explains the difference.

games.q: a friend's dad has a health scare. he says he isn't scared of dying; he's scared he never made peace with his brother. which root is that?
o: regret: good left undone, still waiting to be done.
the body: he's clinging to his health and strength.
doubt: he isn't sure what he believes about death.
games.why: that's the third root: harm done or good left undone. it's also the one root that can still be worked on while he's alive.

practice: Let one fear about death come forward, small enough to hold. Breathe in and ask which root it grows from: wanting, the body, regret or doubt.
Breathe out, and stay beside it kindly, the way you'd sit with a scared kid, without pushing it away.

wordCard.voice: Fear of death: the dread of dying. In this sutta it has four roots, wanting, the body, regret and doubt, and each one can be seen.

orig.note: Pali: fear, dread. The sutta's name, Abhaya, adds a- (not): fearless.

carryVoice: Your line: meet the fear. Fear has roots, and roots can be seen. Two days left in this block.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 4.184 (Abhaya Sutta: Janussoni claims everyone fears death; the Buddha names four who fear and four who don't)
